questions.stem: Which publication do you use to plan a passage through a narrow pass?
options: The chart title block and notes
The current table for that pass and day
The tide table for the nearest port
The weather forecast alone
questions.explanation: Slack water does not necessarily coincide with high or low water, so only the current table gives the times.

questions.stem: The table gives slack at 0750 PST and daylight saving time is in effect. What is slack on the clock?
questions.explanation: Add one hour to standard time in daylight saving time.

questions.stem: Why decide the highest acceptable stream before looking up the times?
options: So your vessel's limit sets the window
Because the limit is set by the harbour authority
Because the table does not list times
Because the limit is the same for every vessel
questions.explanation: Choosing the limit first stops you from stretching the window to suit your schedule. It depends on the boat, the pass and the crew.

questions.stem: A pass entrance is 18.0 nm away. Your speed made good is 6.0 knots and you want to arrive at 1130. When must you leave?
Planned speed made good is 7.5 knots over 18.0 nm and the window is 1512 to 1552. Departure is 1253. If the speed made good turns out to be 5.5 knots, what happens?
options: About 1609, too late: use the waiting plan
She arrives at about 1539, inside the window
She arrives at about 1517 as planned
She arrives at about 1450, before the window
questions.explanation: At 5.5 knots the run takes 18 / 5.5 = 3 h 16 min, so 1253 + 3:16 = 1609. At 7.5 knots she would arrive at 1517 and at 6.5 knots at 1539.

questions.stem: Why aim for the early part of the window and wait outside, rather than the late part?
options: Because waiting outside is not allowed
Because the table is always early
Late means a building stream and no margin
Because slack lasts longer later in the window
questions.explanation: The stream rises after slack. If you are early you wait; if you are late you may meet a stream above your limit.

questions.stem: Why check the wind forecast against the stream direction when planning a pass?
options: Because wind has no effect on a stream
Wind against stream gives short, steep seas
Because wind changes the time of high water by exactly one hour
Because wind makes the stream slower
questions.explanation: Moving water shortens and steepens wind-driven waves, so a wind against the stream makes a steep, confused sea.

questions.stem: The maximum stream is 4.0 knots, 180 minutes after slack, and your limit is 1.0 knot. Using the sine model (stream = maximum x sin of 90 degrees x minutes / 180), about how many minutes either side of slack is the stream below the limit?
options: About 29 minutes
About 15 minutes
About 45 minutes
About 90 minutes
questions.explanation: sin(angle) = 1.0 / 4.0 = 0.25, so the angle is 14.5 degrees. Minutes = 14.5 / 90 x 180 = 29. The model is a teaching approximation, so a real window should be narrower.

questions.stem: The table gives slack, but a strong wind is forecast. What should you assume?
options: Slack will be exactly one hour later
Slack may shift; allow margin, be ready to wait
Slack is unaffected by wind
The pass can be entered at any time
questions.explanation: Strong wind can advance or delay slack water considerably. Secondary stations are also less precise.

questions.stem: What belongs in the plan in case you miss the window?
options: A safe waiting spot and the next slack
Nothing, since slack lasts all day
A decision to enter the pass anyway
Only the time the tide turns
questions.explanation: A plan that cannot be abandoned is a trap. The next slack is hours away and may be in the dark, so the wait must be planned.

questions.stem: At a check fix on the way to the pass, the recalculated ETA falls after the window closes. What do you do?
options: Enter the pass and hope the stream is weak
Cancel the check and trust the original plan
Switch to the waiting plan; don't go on
Increase speed to the maximum and enter anyway
questions.explanation: A go or no-go rule is written before departure. If the ETA is outside the window, the stream will exceed your limit when you arrive.
